detailed_rationale:
Gravita India is India's largest organized secondary-metals recycler, historically anchored in lead recycling (from used lead-acid batteries) and now diversifying into aluminium, plastics, rubber and, most recently, copper. FY26 consolidated revenue was Rs 4,265 crore with consolidated PAT of Rs 378 crore (standalone PAT Rs 297 crore); the company invested Rs 372 crore of capex during the year, expanding lead recycling capacity to 145,100 MTPA, and in March 2026 completed the acquisition of a 98.95% stake in Rashtriya Metal Industries Limited (RMIL, Rs 559 crore) to enter copper and copper-alloy manufacturing at an integrated Gujarat facility, alongside a separate Rs 160 crore new copper-recycling plant investment. Management's stated ambition is to reach over 800,000 MTPA of total capacity by FY2029 — roughly a multi-fold increase from current levels.

The quant data shows revenue growth decelerating (1-year growth 10.3% versus 3-year CAGR 15.0%) even as the balance sheet carries moderate leverage (D/E 0.30x, interest coverage 17.4x) that is set to rise further as the RMIL acquisition and new capacity are funded. This is a business investing heavily ahead of a much larger footprint, which is the right structural bet (organized recyclers are gaining share from the informal sector on environmental-compliance grounds, and battery/EV-linked demand for secondary lead and now copper is a genuine multi-year theme), but it also means near-term revenue growth depends on successful, on-time capacity ramp-up and remains sensitive to metal price cycles (lead, aluminium, copper), which the 'Cyclical' quant tag correctly flags. At ~36x trailing earnings, the market is already paying up for the FY29 capacity vision; execution risk on integrating RMIL and ramping new lines is the main thing to watch, not a demand-side concern.
recommendation_rationale: Quant composite is Hold on both windows and fresh research is consistent with that: the long-term capacity and diversification story (lead to copper, India to a broader international footprint) is genuinely compelling, but recent revenue growth has already decelerated and near-term results depend on executing a large, debt-funded capacity buildout (RMIL, new plants) on schedule while riding through metal-price cyclicality. That combination of real strategic promise plus near-term execution and cyclicality risk is a Hold, not a Sell or an unqualified Buy-equivalent case.
summary: Gravita India is the country's largest organized recycler of lead from used batteries and is expanding aggressively into aluminium, plastics and now copper (via the RMIL acquisition), aiming to multiply its total capacity by FY2029. FY26 results were solid, with consolidated profit of Rs 378 crore, and the long-term case rests on organized recyclers taking share from India's large informal recycling sector. Revenue growth has cooled somewhat from prior years, and the company now needs to successfully integrate a large new acquisition and ramp new capacity while managing metal-price swings. We rate it a Hold: a good structural story, currently in a heavy investment phase.
positive_para: Structural share-shift from India's informal, non-compliant metal-recycling sector to organized, environmentally compliant players like Gravita is a durable, policy-supported tailwind, not a cyclical trade. The FY2029 capacity target (over 800,000 MTPA, versus far less today) backed by the RMIL copper acquisition and new plant investments shows management is actively building the next growth leg beyond legacy lead recycling, diversifying commodity and end-market exposure. Return ratios remain healthy (ROE 22.4%, ROCE 19.6%) even while absorbing a large capex and acquisition program.
negative_para: Revenue growth has already decelerated (10.3% over the last year versus a 15.0% 3-year CAGR), and the company is now layering a large, partly debt-funded acquisition (RMIL, Rs 559 crore) and fresh capacity investment on top of that slower base — execution risk on integration and ramp-up timing is real and unproven at this scale. The 'Cyclical' tag is earned: realized revenue and margins remain sensitive to lead, aluminium and copper price swings regardless of volume growth, so a soft metals cycle could mask genuine volume gains or flatter a weak one, and rising leverage from the acquisition spree bears watching even though current D/E (0.30x) is not yet a red flag.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~36x trailing earnings, the market is pricing a meaningful re-acceleration of growth tied to the FY29 capacity vision and copper diversification, not merely continuation of the recently decelerated ~10% growth. If RMIL integration and new capacity ramp broadly on schedule and metal prices stay constructive, the multiple is defensible; if execution slips or the metals cycle turns, there is limited valuation cushion. Call: fair, contingent on execution — not a clear bargain at current growth trends.

technical_commentary: A strong 2021-2024 uptrend to a Sep-2024 all-time high of Rs2,445 was followed by a genuine -46% correction to a Mar-2026 low of Rs1,318, then 12 months of choppy, directionless back-and-forth in a roughly Rs1,318-1,860 band (currently Rs1,830) with no net progress - a real whipsaw, hence the choppiness flag and penalty. Only 2 of the last 24 months made new highs; despite price nominally sitting above all three monthly averages, the tight bunching reflects a range-bound repair phase rather than a resumed uptrend.
